newsitem.title: ESTONIA: Estonian share market wonders if correction near.
newsitem.headline: Estonian share market wonders if correction near.

text.p: Estonian shares have been on a bull run since the start of the year and analysts and dealers said on Friday they were wondering when the gains would end.
The Tallinn stock exchange has been setting new highs since the start of the year although the rally seemed to run out of steam slightly today.
The index stood at 162.73 on January 2 and ended today at 195.93, down 0.4 percent.
"We are waiting for a correction, it would be very healthy for the stock market," Forekspank dealer Tonu Vanajuur said.
From its start in mid-1996 with a handful of shares, the bourse now lists 15 banks and corporates on three lists.
Analysts attributed the recent price rise to local buyers getting used to the idea of stocks and investing their money on the market, and to foreign investors and low liquidity.
"A fall in prices might take place if investors take their profit," Vanajuur said.
"At the same time, in the second part of January, we expect bank profit forecasts which may lead to a new rally," he said.
He said that most of the gains came without corporate news and that if there was good news then the gains could continue.
Katrin Kaarli, chief analyst at leading bank Hansapank, said she expected more money to flow in from foreign and domestic investors.
She said that investing in stocks had become more popular as more people now knew how the exchange works.

"The Estonian stock market is small, the number of listed shares is not comparable with big stock markets, information is available and it is not so difficult to control your shares without a portfolio manager," Kaarli said.
She said some investors might come to the conclusion that some shares were over-priced and a correction could take place.
So far mostly bank shares have featured on the bourse and dominate trading but corporate shares are catching up.
"Estonian banks are starting to be fairly or fully priced and there may be greater opportunity in bank stocks in Lithuania and Latvia," said Claus Mansfeldt from London-based Nomura Securities.
He said if investors planned to add money to the Estonian market, they would be better to buy non-bank, corporate stocks.
"The corporate side of the market is still holding potential from these levels, but it will be on case-by-case basis," Mansfeldt added.
